rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source considers Judas the more probable identity, noting the Torah names him and inferring he favored Joseph and proposed the well to avoid murder while achieving their aim.
rows.anchor: The Torah also mentions his name. It seems that he had a soft spot in his heart for Joseph (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers follow Judas's advice and report what happened to their father; the succeeding verses describe Jacob's impressions.
rows.anchor: The brothers followed the advice of Judas and reported what happened to their father.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taswīl means making something easy and alluring; Satan's prompting leads a person toward a task by making it seem attractive.
rows.anchor: The word ﺗﺴﻮﻳﻞmeans “to make something easy and luring.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'graceful patience' is an indefinite predicate whose implied point is that it is the best response; it bears sorrow without complaint or unbecoming behavior.
rows.anchor: graceful patience is the best thing to adopt in these circumstances.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's words are an inward reflection, not an address to his sons; the wording 'he said' can carry this sense, and he hopes God will reunite the family.
rows.anchor: the words ascribed to Jacob (sws) in this verse were spoken in his heart and they were not addressed to his sons.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Severe trials heighten hope in God's mercy: devoted servants know God does not test a soul beyond its capacity, so mounting hardship signals approaching help.
rows.anchor: the intensity in trials and tests increases the hope for God’s mercy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob turns away from his sons, becomes saddened, and withdraws in seclusion; the incident revives his grief for Joseph.
rows.anchor: after this incident Jacob became saddened from his sons and isolated himself in a corner.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's grief before God is hopeful and good; crying to God seeks mercy, while forbidden lament is public despair, impatience, and conduct inconsistent with trust.
rows.anchor: Sharing one’s sorrow with God is not a bad thing at all. In fact, it is something good.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Benjamin's case differed from Joseph's, and Jacob's attachment to Joseph reflected his lofty traits; those traits helped provoke his brothers' jealousy.
rows.anchor: the deep attachment which Jacob (sws) had for him was not because he was just his son, but because of his lofty traits.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eyes turning white from intense grief is literal, not exaggeration; grief affects the cornea's darkness and inner parts of the eye.
rows.anchor: this is no expression of exaggeration; it is a statement of fact.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description 'full of anguish' praises Jacob's patience because he kept bearing grief inwardly.
rows.anchor: The word ٌﻢ! ۡﻛﻈﻴ is meant to praise Jacob’s (sws) patience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic tā, as in 'by God,' can mark an oath like wāw; the cited forms also mean 'continually' and a person near death and incapacitated.
rows.anchor: In the Arabic language, تas in !%ٰ ﺗﺎﷲ is also used for an oath the way ﻭis used.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers' apparently sympathetic advice actually reflects the jealousy behind their earlier actions.
rows.anchor: The advice of the brothers cited here though apparently seems sympathetic, it actually smacks of jealousy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers' plot to win their father's attention backfired; they saw his affection for them disappear as he mourned Joseph alone and sought God's help.
rows.anchor: their evil plan had ended up being counter productive.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-bath precisely means worry.
rows.anchor: The precise meaning of the word !%ﺑﺚ is “worry.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Weeping and pleading to God is worship; Jacob tells his sons that his experience and knowledge of God differ from theirs, and that he has not despaired.
rows.anchor: If a person weeps before his Lord, then this nothing bad; in fact, it is a form of worship.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob affectionately urges his sons to search diligently for Joseph and Benjamin, even at risk to themselves, trusting God's mercy to ease their hardships.
rows.anchor: if they try real hard to find Joseph (sws) and Benajamin and even risk their lives for it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term for affliction refers to hardship from hunger and drought; the brothers' offering was a trivial, unwanted provision, apparently goods in kind rather than currency.
rows.anchor: refers to hardship suffered as a result of hunger and drought.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text does not reveal how the father's appeal affected them, but grain need forced another trip to Egypt, where they addressed Joseph by his official title.
rows.anchor: the need for grain forced them to go to Egypt once again.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing his brothers' distress and hearing their earnest plea for charity moved Joseph so deeply that he revealed his identity.
rows.anchor: The situation at hand impacted him so deeply that he decided to reveal his identity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers likely suspected Joseph from his appearance and manner but could not believe a boy cast into a Canaanite well could become Egypt's ruler; those fixed on appearances miss God's power.
rows.anchor: so huge was the disconnect between the well of Canaan in which they had thrown him and the seat of governance he now sat on

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's reply is the anecdote's central essence and forms the sūrah's theme.
rows.anchor: the real essence of the whole anecdote and it actually forms the theme of the sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iḥsān, understood as thoroughness, is a prerequisite for accepted God-consciousness and steadfastness: worship with awareness that God sees you, even when you do not see Him.
rows.anchor: only that fear of God and steadfastness is acceptable to Him which has the essence of a person being thorough

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers' admission recognizes that their resentment came from their father's preference for Joseph, while God's preference exposed their error and affirmed Joseph's deserving status.
rows.anchor: God by giving him this preference made them realize their mistake.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb for blame means reproaching someone for a blameworthy deed; sincere regret makes forgiveness from noble Joseph and, one may hope, God appropriate.
rows.anchor: If someone accepts his mistake with true regret, a person as noble as Joseph (sws) is bound to forgive him

rows.speaker: Prophet Muḥammad (sws)
rows.claim: At the conquest of Makkah, the Prophet used Joseph's words to release the Quraysh leaders who had been his enemies; they called him a courteous brother and son of a courteous brother.
rows.anchor: these words were also uttered by Prophet Muḥammad (sws) at the conquest of Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shirt is a remedy for Jacob's grief-weakened eyes because it brings overwhelming joy; Benjamin had told Joseph how much Jacob's eyesight had declined.
rows.anchor: The sole remedy for the eyes that have become weak because of grief and weeping

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shirt reverses the emotional role of the earlier blood-stained garment: Joseph's false death caused Jacob's greatest sorrow, and this garment brings his greatest joy.
rows.anchor: the greatest sorrow inflicted on Jacob (sws) was through the shirt of Joseph (sws) which was stained with fake blood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shirt's effect reflects the emotions of Joseph and Jacob; the marvels of such pure feeling can take forms the intellect cannot explain.
rows.anchor: the marvels of the effects of such pure emotions manifest themselves in such amazing forms that intellect is unable to decipher them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the verse does not name the parents, they are understood; summoning them is the real purpose, with the rest of the family secondary.
rows.anchor: the real purpose was to call them. The rest of the lot was secondary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faṣala means to depart; tafnīd means deeming someone foolish and therefore dismissing their opinion.
rows.anchor: The verb !!!ﻓﺼﻞ means “to depart from a place.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophet's senses and faculties should not be compared to ours; even ordinary people can perceive more deeply in crisis, so Jacob detecting his son's scent is unsurprising.
rows.anchor: the senses and faculties of the individuals God chooses as His prophets and messengers should not be considered analogous to our senses and faculties.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people's words are exactly what Jacob had anticipated when he expressed his claim in the previous verse.
rows.anchor: These words were precisely the ones Jacob (sws) had anticipated and feared

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A verb is understood as omitted in the expression about the bearer of good news arriving.
rows.anchor: a verb is supressed after the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's statement that he knows what others do not refers back to verse 86; its fulfillment teaches his sons not to be captive to appearances but to trust the divine workings hidden within them.
rows.anchor: they must not lead their lives while being slaves to the apparent; they should also have faith in what is hidden in this apparent from among the acts of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After seeing events unfold, the brothers recognize their folly, confess their sin to Jacob as they had to Joseph, and ask him to seek forgiveness.
rows.anchor: they had confessed their mistake before Joseph (sws), as referred to in verse 91

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's 'soon' promises a focused prayer for their forgiveness at a particular time rather than an immediate general supplication.
rows.anchor: The word !ۡ!ﺳﻮف soon) refers to the fact that Jacob (sws) had promised to supplicate for them with special focus at a particular time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sinner ashamed of wrongdoing may ask the righteous to pray for him; focused supplication at a particular time and place can also contribute to its acceptance.
rows.anchor: if a person is ashamed of his sins, he can also ask the righteous to supplicate for him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative omits, by contextual indication, the family's arrival in Egypt in compliance with Joseph's order; his words welcome his parents.
rows.anchor: the brothers and their parents along with their own families reached Egypt in compliance with the orders of Joseph (sws).

rows.speaker: Bible
rows.claim: The Bible says Joseph came out of the city to welcome his arriving family and escorted them in such splendor that their arrival became a festive occasion.
rows.anchor: According to the Bible, when they arrived, Joseph (sws) welcomed them by coming out of the city

rows.speaker: Bible
rows.claim: The Bible indicates Joseph's mother had died and he was raised by his stepmother, his paternal aunt; the expression for his parents uses the dominant element.
rows.anchor: it is evident from the Bible that Joseph’s mother had passed away.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The throne is the seat Joseph used to decide cases and disputes, not necessarily a royal throne; ministers and senior officials also sat on thrones.
rows.anchor: The “throne” here does not refer to the royal throne but to the throne on which Joseph (sws) would sit to decide various cases and disputes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kharra means falling from above to below; sajdah here is reverential bowing, of which putting the forehead on the ground is the fullest form rather than a necessary element.
rows.anchor: prostration here means to bow in respect; placing one’s forhead on the ground is not its essential part

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah presents this form of honoring elders as common, usually kneeling; even a ceremonial prostration is not polytheism in itself, though Islam prohibits such forms and expressions.
rows.anchor: it was of the form of kneeling and not prostration. If someone inteprets this word to mean prostration in the ceremonial sense, even then it does not make any difference because prostration per se does not constitute polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph seated his parents near him as respect; his courtiers and attendees then bowed according to custom, and the others followed spontaneously.
rows.anchor: Joseph (sws) shared his throne with his parents as a mark of respect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode testifies that God's knowledge and wisdom create subtle routes to fruition that people cannot imagine.
rows.anchor: God creates such subtle ways of fruition for certain tasks through His knowledge and wisdom that cannot even be imagined.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's heart fills with gratitude as he sees what has happened, prompting his supplication.
rows.anchor: Joseph’s (sws) heart becomes replete with gratitude when he sees what has happened

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing passage reassures the Prophet and warns the Quraysh to learn from earlier nations or face their fate.
rows.anchor: In them, the Prophet (sws) is addressed and given assurance; at the same time, the Quraysh are threatened

none: A surah title page only; no commentary.
Publisher copyright notice only; no commentary text.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's task is to deliver the message; God determines who accepts faith and gives each person what they deserve.
rows.anchor: his responsibility is to only deliver the message.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 5–17 present Moses and other messengers facing hardship, persevering, and ultimately prevailing; the Prophet and companions should persist first and show gratitude in the final phase.
rows.anchor: ultimately they too will remain dominant in this conflict. But they must show perseverance in the initial phases and gratitude in the last phase.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 18–22 depict disbelievers' efforts vanishing, followed by leaders, followers, and Satan disowning and cursing one another.
rows.anchor: All their efforts will end up in vain and will just vanish in the air.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 23–27 contrast the disbelievers with believers who greet one another and succeed in both worlds through God's profound and forceful word.
rows.anchor: the believers in the hereafter will greet and congratulate each other.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 28–34 warn Quraysh leaders that they turned God's favors into grounds for disbelief and led their people to Hell; Muslims are urged to pray and give charity.
rows.anchor: used God’s favours a means for their disbelief and polytheism and in this way led their people to Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's prayers concern Makkah and his children settled there, showing Quraysh that their lives oppose his hopes while Muhammad and his followers fulfill them.
rows.anchor: The purpose is to make evident to the Quraysh that the whole life that they are leading is totally against the supplications and desires of Abraham (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah's concluding section, verses 42–52, is filled with warnings.
rows.anchor: This concluding section of the sūrah is replete with warnings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'your Lord' shows that the address is directed to the people being addressed.
rows.anchor: the words “your Lord” clearly show that it was addressed to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses clarifies that God does not need human gratitude; gratitude benefits people by bringing an increase in God's favors.
rows.anchor: this attitude of gratitude is instrumental in producing blessings for them actually because, as pointed out earlier, it makes God increase His favours upon people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section is generally phrased but addresses Muslims, assuring them that messengers endured severe hardship, even exile, yet believers ultimately succeed.
rows.anchor: The address in this section is though general but it is directed at the Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nations older than Noah's people, ʿĀd, and Thamūd are not named in the verse.
rows.anchor: The nations which lived earlier than the ones mentioned have not been named.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No reliable historical account identifies the unnamed nations; only God knows them, as also indicated by 40:78.
rows.anchor: There is no reliable mention of them in history too. Only God knows about them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording about placing hands on mouths means the people tried to silence their messengers out of hatred and anger; the term is idiomatic.
rows.anchor: they tried to shut the mouths of their messengers. This is what happens when a person out of hate and anger tries to stop someone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers' question expresses wonder: their audience itself accepts God as creator, and the messengers call only to Him; rejection of other deities has no counterargument.
rows.anchor: This question posed by the messengers is out of wonder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's choosing a messenger does not mean arbitrary selection; wisdom grants the position only to those worthy of it. Miracles are in God's authority, so believers should trust Him.
rows.anchor: He confers this position only on those who are worthy of it in accordance with His wisdom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers trust God to guide and help them through obstacles; their role is to persevere and trust Him, including when asked for a miracle.
rows.anchor: it is their faith that God will help and guide them through the hindrances and hardships they face for this cause.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every messenger faces threats of expulsion or forced return, followed by God's promise of their people's destruction and the messengers' inheritance of the land.
rows.anchor: This phase has ensued in the life of every messenger that their people have warned them in the words stated in the verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat that messengers return to their people's way does not mean they previously followed jāhiliyyah; before appointment they follow the religion of their innate nature, and condemnation starts when they preach.
rows.anchor: Even before being called to this position, God’s messengers follow the religion ingrained in their nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The followers, too, receive glad tidings only if they endure hardship bravely and fear God above their enemies.
rows.anchor: they are warned that they will only reap these blessings if they bravely face hardships

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage indicates a time when Quraysh oppression had made migration from the homeland unavoidable for the Prophet and believers.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh had oppressed the Prophet (sws) and the believers so much that they had no option but to migrate from their homeland.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers repeatedly demanded the threatened punishment, while messengers continued hoping for their people's guidance until their patience reached a limit and they prayed for judgment.
rows.anchor: The believers repeatedly demanded from their messengers to bring the punishment they continuously threaten them with.
